issues.legal_issue: A disciplinary finding warranting disbarment cannot stand when the evidence leaves reasonable doubt about professional misconduct.
material_facts: The advocate admitted receiving money but disputed that it had been paid to file a suit, and said it was part payment of a fee for proposed work.

The complainant’s account had inconsistencies: the suit number and amount on the plaint copy had been filled in later, the claimed court fee did not match the amount paid, and the complaint was made after a substantial delay.
The evidence left doubt about whether the complainant’s account was truthful and whether the dispute concerned payment for work performed.
The disciplinary committee relied in part on prior complaints and the advocate’s history, which the Court considered capable of prejudicing its assessment of the present allegations.
The disciplinary committee found professional misconduct and permanently disbarred the advocate.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and the order permanently disbarring the advocate was set aside because the evidence did not exclude reasonable doubt about guilt.
issues.legal_principle: In a professional misconduct proceeding that may result in disbarment, the evidence must be of a character that leaves no reasonable doubt about guilt. The tribunal must assess the evidence in the particular case without allowing an accused professional’s background or prior complaints to create prejudice. Section 36B of the Advocates Act, 1961, was mentioned as the basis for transferring the complaint after the State Bar Council did not dispose of it within six months, but it did not supply the evidentiary standard applied on appeal. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for this standard.

predicates.disciplinary_appeal: The matter is an appeal from a decision in a professional disciplinary proceeding.
predicates.disbarment_imposed: The disciplinary body imposed disbarment for alleged professional misconduct.
predicates.evidence_leaves_reasonable_doubt: The evidence supporting the misconduct finding leaves reasonable doubt about whether the professional committed the misconduct.
predicates.disbarment_order_set_aside: The disbarment order is set aside.

issues.definition: When a professional appeals a disbarment imposed in disciplinary proceedings and the evidence leaves reasonable doubt about the alleged misconduct, the disbarment order is set aside.
